facts: Python is named after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.
In 1947, a moth found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II was taped into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found."
The first website, published by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, went live in 1991.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email in 1971 and picked the @ symbol to separate user and host.
Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 after the Linux kernel lost free access to BitKeeper.
The first computer mouse prototype, built by Douglas Engelbart's team in the 1960s, had a wooden shell.
Unix time counts seconds from January 1, 1970. Signed 32-bit timestamps overflow on January 19, 2038.
Ada Lovelace published what is widely regarded as the first algorithm intended for a machine in 1843.
JavaScript was prototyped by Brendan Eich in about ten days in 1995.
symbolics.com, registered on March 15, 1985, is considered the first .com domain.
Google's search engine was originally called BackRub.
The Apollo Guidance Computer had roughly 4 KB of erasable memory.
The perceptron, an ancestor of modern neural networks, was introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958.
The term "machine learning" is credited to Arthur Samuel, who used it in 1959 for his checkers-playing program at IBM.
IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997.
The first ARPANET message in 1969 was meant to be "LOGIN" but the system crashed after "LO."
The "Hello, World!" program was popularized by the book The C Programming Language by Kernighan and Ritchie.
The smiley :-) was proposed on a Carnegie Mellon message board by Scott Fahlman in 1982.
Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united tribes.
CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.
Rwanda was one of the first countries where Zipline began delivering blood by drone, starting in 2016.
In 2012, the neural network AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin and helped kick off the deep learning boom.
The word "bit", short for binary digit, was popularized by Claude Shannon in 1948 and credited to John Tukey.
Linus Torvalds announced Linux in 1991 as "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu."
